Frederick Douglass - model: the Italics in Webster's Spelling Book, the letters marked on ship-yard timber (L, S, L. F., S. F., L. A., S. A.), and what Master Thomas had written in his copy-books
Frederick Douglass - practice: used a board fence, brick wall, and pavement as copy-book and a lump of chalk as pen and ink; challenged boys who could write to beat his letters; wrote in the spaces left in Master Thomas's copy-books when his mistress was at class meeting on Monday afternoons
Benjamin Franklin - model: NOT_FOUND
Benjamin Franklin - practice: did writing exercises and reading at night after work or before it began in the morning, or on Sundays when he contrived to be in the printing-house alone

Douglass practised by copying specific models (Webster's Italics, ship-yard letters, Master Thomas's handwriting) using chalk on fences, walls, and pavement, while Franklin practised through writing exercises done in his spare time at night, early morning, or Sundays alone in the printing-house; the evidence does not state what model Franklin used.

Faraday explains that the candle's heat creates an ascending current of air that cools the outer edges, keeping them solid while the interior melts. Points:

1. As air comes to the candle it moves upwards by the force of the current which the heat of the candle produces, cooling all the sides of the wax, tallow, or fuel, so the edge stays much cooler than the part within (evidence [2]).
2. The part within melts by the flame that runs down the wick as far as it can go before it is extinguished, but the part on the outside does not melt (evidence [2]).
3. This beautifully regular ascending current of air playing upon all sides keeps the exterior of the candle cool and forms the cup; if the current is one-sided, the cup becomes lop-sided and the fluid runs over in guttering (evidence [1]).
4. No fuel would serve for a candle which has not the property of giving this cup, except such fuel as the Irish bogwood, where the material itself is like a sponge and holds its own fuel (evidence [1], [4]).
Mr. Johnson chose the surname "Douglass," suggested by the "Lady of the Lake," which he had just been reading.

Order was the hardest virtue for Franklin to acquire.

- Its number and precept: it is number 3 in his list, with the precept "Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time" (Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection, list of virtues).
- Reason 1: he had not been early accustomed to it, having an exceeding good memory, so he was not sensible of the inconvenience of want of method (Order passage).
- Reason 2: as a master who must mix with the world, he often received people of business at their own hours, which interfered with it.
- Result: it cost him painful attention, his faults vexed him, he made little progress and had frequent relapses, and he remained "incorrigible with respect to Order," feeling the want of it even in old age.

Douglass learned to read in Baltimore through his mistress's initial teaching, Mr. Auld's prohibition, and then his own clever stratagems with white boys.

- Mrs. Auld first taught him: she kindly commenced to teach him the A, B, C, and then helped him spell words of three or four letters (Chapter VI).
- Mr. Auld found out and at once forbade her to continue, saying it was unlawful as well as unsafe to teach a slave to read (Chapter VI).
- His reasons: "If you give a nigger an inch, he will take an ell"; learning would spoil the best slave, forever unfit him to be a slave, make him unmanageable and of no value to his master, and make him discontented and unhappy (Chapter VI).
- Afterward, Douglass had no regular teacher, so he made friends of little white boys he met in the street and converted them into teachers, carrying his book on errands and trading bread for lessons, until he finally succeeded in learning to read (Chapter VII).

Faraday makes the water visible by placing a chimney over the burning candle: the moisture appearing on it is water produced from the candle by the action of the air upon its hydrogen (passage [1]).

He shows the presence of carbonic acid in two ways. First, the air coming out of the top of the chimney is nearly sufficient to blow out a light held to it, and will blow it quite out if opposed to the current (passage [1]); the same effect is later produced by gas from the candle itself, showing it is "caused by the very same substance that issued from the candle" (passage [5]). Second, he applies lime-water as a test: water impregnated with carbonic acid makes the lime-water turbid and white, which is proof of its presence (passage [3]); the lime combines with something from the candle to form a white powder exactly the same as whitening or chalk (passage [2]).

Franklin's father made candles from tallow, which Faraday explains is the fat of the ox (Russian tallow, used for making dips). To turn it into stearin, the fat or tallow is first boiled with quick-lime to make a soap, and then the soap is decomposed by sulphuric acid, which takes away the lime and leaves the fat re-arranged as stearic acid, with glycerin produced at the same time; the oil is then pressed out, leaving the substance that is melted and cast into candles.

Benjamin Franklin - apprentice indentures: twelve years old
Frederick Douglass - leaving Colonel Lloyd's plantation for Baltimore: probably between seven and eight years old

Franklin was twelve when bound to his brother, while Douglass was between seven and eight when sent to Baltimore, so Douglass was younger at that turning point.
